cases.question: Tell me about Prussian education system.
cases.answer: The Prussian education system was a comprehensive and compulsory system that provided free public education for everyone, but with significantly higher fees for attending gymnasium or a university, imposing a high barrier between upper social strata and middle and lower social strata [n]. The system was based on the Humboldtian educational ideal, which strived for academic freedom and the education of both cosmopolitan-minded and loyal citizens from the earliest levels [n]. The system was mainly tripartite, with three types of schools: the primary school, the gymnasium, and the university [n]. The primary school provided basic education, the gymnasium provided advanced education, and the university provided higher education [n]. The system was influential in shaping the modern nation-state and was widely admired for its efficiency and reduction of illiteracy [n].

cases.question: Tell me about Signage.
cases.answer:
Signage is the design or use of signs and symbols to communicate a message. A signage also means signs collectively or being considered as a group. The term signage is documented to have been popularized in 1975 to 1980 [1]. Signs are any kind of visual graphics created to display information to a particular audience [1]. This is typically manifested in the form of wayfinding information in places such as streets or on the inside and outside buildings [1]. Signs vary in form and size based on location and intent, from more expansive banners, billboards, and murals, to smaller street signs, street name signs, sandwich boards and lawn signs [1]. Newer signs may also use digital or electronic displays [1]. The main purpose of signs is to communicate, to convey information designed to assist the receiver with decision-making based on the information provided [1]. Alternatively, promotional signage may be designed to persuade receivers of the merits of a given product or service [1]. Signage is distinct from labeling, which conveys information about a particular product or service [1].

The term, 'sign' comes from the old French signe (noun), signer (verb), meaning a gesture or a motion of the hand [1]. This, in turn, stems from Latin 'signum' indicating an"identifying mark, token, indication, symbol; proof; military standard, ensign; a signal, an omen; sign in the heavens, constellation" [1]. In the English, the term is also associated with a flag or ensign [1]. In France, a banner not infrequently took the place of signs or sign boards in the Middle Ages [1]. Signs, however, are best known in the form of painted or carved , inns, cinemas, etc. [1]. They are one of various emblematic methods for publicly calling attention to the place to which they refer [1].

Signs perform the following roles or functions: Information-provision: signs conveying information about services and facilities, such as maps, directories, instructional signs or interpretive signage used in museums, galleries, zoos, parks and gardens, exhibitions, tourist and cultural attractions that enhance the customer's experience [2]. Retail signage state product names or simply the prices [2]. Persuasion: promotional signage designed to persuade users of the relative merits of a company, product or brand [2]. Direction/ Navigation: signs showing the location of services, facilities, functional spaces and key areas, such as sign posts or directional arrows [2]. Identification: signs indicating services and facilities, such as room names and numbers, restroom signs, or floor designations [2]. Safety and Regulatory: signs giving warning or safety instructions, such as warning signs, traffic signs, exit signs, signs indicating what to do in an emergency or natural disaster or signs conveying rules and regulations [2].

Signs may be used in exterior spaces or on-premises locations [2]. Signs used on the exterior of a building are often designed to encourage people to enter and on the interior to encourage people to explore the environment and participate in all that the space has to offer [2]. Any given sign may perform multiple roles simultaneously [2]. For example, signage may provide information, but may also serve to assist customers navigate their way through a complex service or retail environment [2].

Pictograms are images commonly used to convey the message of a sign [3]. In statutory signage, pictograms follow specific sets of colour, shape and sizing rules based on the laws of the country in which the signage is being displayed [3]. For example, In UK and EU signage, the width of a sign's pictogram must be 80% the height of the area it is printed to [3]. In the US, in order to comply with the ADA Accessibility Guidelines, the same pictogram must be located within its own defined field, with raised characters and braille located beneath the field [3]. For a pictogram to be successful it must be recognizable across cultures and languages, even if there is no text present [3]. Following standard color and shape conventions increases the likelihood that the pictogram and sign will be universally understood [3].

The shape of a sign can help to convey its message [3]. Shape can be brand- or design-based, or can be part of a set of signage conventions used to standardize sign meaning [3]. Usage of particular shapes may vary by country and culture [3]. Some common signage shape conventions are as follows: Rectangular signs are often used to portray general information to an audience [3]. Circular signs often represent an instruction that must be followed, either mandatory or prohibitive [3]. Triangular signs are often warning signs, used to convey danger or caution [3].

Signs frequently use lighting as a means of conveying their information or as a way to increase visibility [5]. Neon signs, introduced in 1910 at the Paris Motor Show, are produced by the craft of bending glass tubing into shapes [5].

cases.question: Tell me about Polar Bear (British band).
cases.answer: Polar Bear is a British experimental jazz band led by drummer Seb Rochford with Pete Wareham and Mark Lockheart on tenor saxophone, Tom Herbert on double bass and Leafcutter John on electronics and occasionally guitar or mandolin [1]. They were nominated for the Best Band award at the BBC Jazz Awards 2004, while Rochford was nominated for the 'Rising Star' award [1]. Their first album Dim Lit was released in the same year and was a small scale success [1]. Their second record, Held on the Tips of Fingers merged elements of cool jazz, funk, dance music, free jazz, electronica and drum and bass and was, by comparison, a crossover hit, earning Polar Bear a nomination for the Mercury Music Prize in 2005 [1]. The success was all the more unusual for an almost purely instrumental album [1]. The album was nominated for a BBC Jazz Award 2006 [1]. It was selected as one of "The 100 Jazz Albums That Shook The World" by Jazzwise magazine [1]. and featured in The Guardian's list of "1000 Albums To Hear Before You Die" [1]. They have been involved with F-IRE Collective [1]. They released their self-titled third album, Polar Bear, in July 2008 with Tin Angel Records [1]. In 2010, the band released Peepers and mini-album Common Ground, a collaboration with Portuguese-born, London-based rapper Jyager, on The Leaf Label [1]. Their 2014 album In Each And Every One was shortlisted for the Mercury Music Prize and in the same year they released the single "Cuckoo" in collaboration with singer and songwriter Jin Jin [1]. In March 2015 Polar Bear released their sixth album Same as You, including the single "Don't Let The Feeling Go" [1]. This track features frequent collaborator Shabaka Hutchings (Sons of Kemet and The Comet Is Coming) on tenor saxophone and Rochford and Hannah Darling on vocals [1]. In 2015, Polar Bear were nominated for Best Jazz Act in the MOBO Awards and Urban Music Awards [1].

Their second record, Held on the Tips of Fingers merged elements of cool jazz, funk, dance music, free jazz, electronica and drum and bass and was, by comparison, a crossover hit, earning Polar Bear a nomination for the Mercury Music Prize in 2005.
The success was all the more unusual for an almost purely instrumental album.
The album was nominated for a BBC Jazz Award 2006.
It was selected as one of "The 100 Jazz Albums That Shook The World" by Jazzwise magazine. and featured in The Guardian's list of "1000 Albums To Hear Before You Die".
They have been involved with F-IRE Collective.
They released their self-titled third album, Polar Bear, in July 2008 with Tin Angel Records.
In 2010, the band released Peepers and mini-album Common Ground, a collaboration with Portuguese-born, London-based rapper Jyager, on The Leaf Label.
Their 2014 album In Each And Every One was shortlisted for the Mercury Music Prize and in the same year they released the single "Cuckoo" in collaboration with singer and songwriter Jin Jin.
In March 2015 Polar Bear released their sixth album Same as You, including the single "Don't Let The Feeling Go".
This track features frequent collaborator Shabaka Hutchings (Sons of Kemet and The Comet Is Coming) on tenor saxophone and Rochford and Hannah Darling on vocals.
In 2015, Polar Bear were nominated for Best Jazz Act in the MOBO Awards and Urban Music Awards.
